claim: Kymographs are graphical representations of spatial position over time.
source: Kymographs are graphical representations of spatial position over time, which are often used in biology to visualise the motion of fluorescent particles, molecules, vesicles, or organelles moving along a predictable path.
evidence: This is a definitional statement presented in the abstract.

claim: Kymographs are often used in biology to visualise the motion of fluorescent particles, molecules, vesicles, or organelles moving along a predictable path.
source: Kymographs are graphical representations of spatial position over time, which are often used in biology to visualise the motion of fluorescent particles, molecules, vesicles, or organelles moving along a predictable path.
evidence: This describes the common application of kymographs in biological research.

claim: Kymographs often exhibit low signal-to-noise-ratios (SNRs).
source: Kymographs often exhibit low signal-to-noise-ratios (SNRs), and available tools that automate their analysis usually require manual supervision.
evidence: This is a general observation about the characteristics of kymographs.

claim: Available tools that automate kymograph analysis usually require manual supervision.
source: Kymographs often exhibit low signal-to-noise-ratios (SNRs), and available tools that automate their analysis usually require manual supervision.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of existing automated tools.

claim: KymoButler is a Deep Learning-based software to automatically track dynamic processes in kymographs.
source: Here we developed KymoButler, a Deep Learning-based software to automatically track dynamic processes in kymographs.
evidence: This describes the nature and purpose of the developed software.

claim: KymoButler performs as well as expert manual data analysis on kymographs with complex particle trajectories from a variety of different biological systems.
source: We demonstrate that KymoButler performs as well as expert manual data analysis on kymographs with complex particle trajectories from a variety of different biological systems.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on benchmarking experiments.

claim: The KymoButler software was packaged in a web-based 'one-click' application available at https://deepmirror.ai/kymobutler.
source: The software was packaged in a web-based 'one-click' application for use by the wider scientific community (https://deepmirror.ai/kymobutler).
evidence: This describes the deployment and accessibility of the software.

claim: KymoButler significantly speeds up data analysis.
source: Our approach significantly speeds up data analysis, avoids unconscious bias, and represents another step towards the widespread adaptation of Machine Learning techniques in biological data analysis.
evidence: This is a claimed advantage of the software based on comparison with manual analysis.

claim: KymoButler avoids unconscious bias.
source: Our approach significantly speeds up data analysis, avoids unconscious bias, and represents another step towards the widespread adaptation of Machine Learning techniques in biological data analysis.
evidence: This is a claimed advantage of automated analysis over manual annotation.

claim: Particle tracking algorithms represent powerful approaches to track the dynamics of particles.
source: Particle tracking algorithms represent powerful approaches to track the dynamics of such particles (Jaqaman et al., 2008; Sbalzarini and Koumoutsakos, 2005; Lee and Park, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Molecules transported along neuronal axons, dendrites, or along cilia typically move along the structure's long axis and do not show significant motion perpendicular to that path.
source: For example, molecules transported along neuronal axons, dendrites, or along cilia typically move along the structure's long axis and do not show significant motion perpendicular to that path.
evidence: This describes the characteristic motion pattern of particles in specific biological contexts.

claim: Retrograde actin flow typically occurs along a single axis within the cell.
source: Similarly, retrograde actin flow typically occurs along a single axis within the cell.
evidence: This describes the characteristic motion pattern of retrograde actin flow.

claim: Kymographs have been widely employed to visualise biological processes across different length scales, ranging from diffusion and transport of single molecules to whole cell movements.
source: Hence, kymographs have been widely employed to visualise biological processes across different length scales, ranging from diffusion and transport of single molecules to whole cell movements (Twelvetrees et al., 2016; Barry et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Publicly available kymograph analysis software simplifies the tedious and time-consuming task of tracing kymographs, but most of these solutions require manual supervision and/or high signal to noise ratios.
source: Publicly available kymograph analysis software simplifies the tedious and time-consuming task of tracing kymographs, but most of these solutions require manual supervision and/or high signal to noise ratios (Neumann et al., 2017; Mangeol et al., 2016; Chenouard, 2010; Zala et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to existing software tools.

claim: Existing kymograph analysis tools perform reasonably well when applied to particles with unidirectional motion and uniform velocities.
source: These tools perform reasonably well when applied to particles with unidirectional motion and uniform velocities as, for example, growing microtubule +ends (Figure 1C, example 2) and F-actin dynamics in retrograde actin flow (Lazarus et al., 2013; del Castillo et al., 2015; Alexandrova et al., 2008; Babich et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations and references to figures.

claim: In many biological contexts, particles can stop moving, change velocity, change direction, merge, cross each other's path, or disappear for a few frames.
source: In many other biological contexts, however, particles can stop moving, change velocity, change direction, merge, cross each other's path, or disappear for a few frames.
evidence: This describes the complexity of particle dynamics in certain biological systems.

claim: Most kymographs are still analysed by hand, which is slow and prone to unconscious bias.
source: Thus, the problem of automatically and reliably tracking dynamic processes in kymographs still leaves substantial room for improvement, and given the limitations of currently available kymograph analysis software, most kymographs are still analysed by hand, which is slow and prone to unconscious bias.
evidence: This is a statement about current practice in the field.

claim: Machine Learning, and particularly Deep Neural Networks, have been very successfully introduced to data processing in biology and medicine.
source: In recent years, Machine Learning (ML), and particularly Deep Neural Networks, have been very successfully introduced to data processing in biology and medicine (Mathis, 2018; Weigert, 2017; Florian, 2017; Guerrero-Pena, 2018; Falk et al., 2019; Bates, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: ML-based image analysis is less susceptible to bias than manual annotation.
source: ML-based image analysis has several advantages over other approaches: it is less susceptible to bias than manual annotation, it takes a much shorter time to analyse large datasets, and, most importantly, it comes closer to human performance than conventional algorithms (Mathis, 2018).
evidence: This is a claimed advantage of ML-based approaches, supported by citation.

claim: ML-based image analysis takes a much shorter time to analyse large datasets than manual annotation.
source: ML-based image analysis has several advantages over other approaches: it is less susceptible to bias than manual annotation, it takes a much shorter time to analyse large datasets, and, most importantly, it comes closer to human performance than conventional algorithms (Mathis, 2018).
evidence: This is a claimed advantage of ML-based approaches, supported by citation.

claim: ML-based image analysis comes closer to human performance than conventional algorithms.
source: ML-based image analysis has several advantages over other approaches: it is less susceptible to bias than manual annotation, it takes a much shorter time to analyse large datasets, and, most importantly, it comes closer to human performance than conventional algorithms (Mathis, 2018).
evidence: This is a claimed advantage of ML-based approaches, supported by citation.

claim: Fully Convolutional Deep Neural Networks (FCNs) excel at object detection in images.
source: Most ML approaches to image analysis utilise Fully Convolutional Deep Neural Networks (FCNs) that were shown to excel at object detection in images (Dai, 2016; Szegedy, 2014; LeCun et al., 1989; Falk et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The U-Net is currently the most successful architecture for biological and medical image analysis.
source: Currently, the most successful architecture for biological and medical image analysis is the U-Net, which takes an input image to generate a binary map that highlights objects of interest based on the training data (Ronneberger et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation.

claim: KymoButler is based on the U-Net architecture.
source: Here we present KymoButler, a new stand-alone FCN software based on the U-Net architecture, to automatically and reliably extract particle tracks from kymographs.
evidence: This describes the architectural basis of the developed software.

claim: KymoButler was benchmarked against traditional software and manual annotation on synthetic and real biological data.
source: The software is packaged into an easy-to-use web interface (https://deepmirror.ai/kymobutler) and a downloadable software package, and it was benchmarked against traditional software and manual annotation on synthetic (i.e., ground truth) and real (biological) data.
evidence: This describes the evaluation methodology used in the study.

claim: KymoButler performs as well as manual annotation on challenging bidirectional kymographs.
source: We show that KymoButler performs as well as manual annotation on challenging bidirectional kymographs, where particles disappear, reappear, merge, cross each other's path, move in any direction, change speed, immobilise, and reverse direction.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on benchmarking experiments.

claim: KymoButler speeds up the experimental workflow while preserving the accuracy of manual annotations.
source: KymoButler thus represents a substantial improvement in the automation of kymograph tracing, speeding up the experimental workflow, while preserving the accuracy of manual annotations.
evidence: This is a summary claim about the benefits of the software.

claim: KymoButler comprises two segmentation networks, one specialised on kymographs with exclusively unidirectional particle movements, the other on bi-directional kymographs.
source: This architecture comprises two segmentation networks ('modules'), one specialised on kymographs with exclusively unidirectional particle movements, the other one on bi-directional kymographs.
evidence: This describes the modular architecture of the software.

claim: The segmentation networks were trained to binarize the image into regions with particle tracks (foreground) and noise (background).
source: These segmentation networks were trained to binarize the image into regions with particle tracks (foreground) and noise (background).
evidence: This describes the function of the segmentation networks.

claim: The segmentation networks generate 2D maps that assign a 'trackness' value between 0 and 1 to each pixel of the input image.
source: They take an input kymograph to generate 2D maps that assign a 'trackness' value between 0 and 1 to each pixel of the input image, with higher values representing a higher likelihood of pixels being part of a track (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the output of the segmentation networks.

claim: The training and validation data consisted of manually annotated tracks in 487 unidirectional and 79 bidirectional kymographs.
source: Our training (95%) and validation (5%) data consisted of manually annotated tracks in 487 unidirectional and 79 bidirectional kymographs (unpublished data from our group and other laboratories, see Materials and methods and Acknowledgements for details).
evidence: This describes the composition of the training dataset.

claim: 221 synthetic unidirectional and 21 synthetic bidirectional kymographs were generated and used for training.
source: Since no ground truth was available in the manually annotated kymographs, we also generated 221 synthetic unidirectional and 21 synthetic bidirectional kymographs that were used for training.
evidence: This describes the synthetic data generation for training.

claim: The unidirectional segmentation module generates separate trackness maps for tracks with negative and positive slopes.
source: The unidirectional segmentation module generates separate trackness maps for tracks with negative and positive slopes (which could, for example, correspond to tracks of anterograde and retrograde transport processes, respectively), to remove line crossings from the output (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the specific functionality of the unidirectional module.

claim: The bidirectional segmentation module generates a single trackness map.
source: In bidirectional kymographs, tracks show more complex morphologies, since they can change direction/speed and cross each other multiple times. The bidirectional segmentation module therefore generates a single trackness map, which needs to be further processed in order to obtain individual particle tracks.
evidence: This describes the specific functionality of the bidirectional module.

claim: A decision module was implemented to resolve crossings between tracks in bidirectional kymographs.
source: In particular, one has to resolve crossings between tracks. We did this by implementing a decision module which iterates through all crossings to find the most likely final segmentation (see Materials and methods for details).
evidence: This describes the implementation of the decision module.

claim: The best performance for both segmentation modules was generally observed for binarization threshold values between 0.1–0.3.
source: We found the binarization thresholds for both modules to depend on the biological application and on the signal to noise ratio of the input image. However, we observed the best performance for both segmentation modules generally for values between 0.1–0.3 (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is based on empirical testing shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: A classification module was implemented to classify input kymographs into unidirectional or bidirectional ones.
source: Finally, our software has to decide whether to analyse a given kymograph with the unidirectional module or the bidirectional module. Therefore, we implemented a 'classification module' that classifies input kymographs into unidirectional or bidirectional ones.
evidence: This describes the implementation of the classification module.

claim: The only free parameter in KymoButler is the threshold for trackness map segmentation.
source: The only free parameter in KymoButler is the threshold for trackness map segmentation.
evidence: This describes the user-adjustable parameters of the software.

claim: The default threshold in KymoButler is set to 0.2.
source: The default threshold is set to 0.2, but users can freely adjust it for their specific application.
evidence: This describes the default parameter setting.

claim: KymoButler takes 1–20 s per kymograph to complete computation.
source: After the computation, which takes 1–20 s per kymograph (depending on complexity), KymoButler generates several files including a dilated overlay image highlighting all the tracks found in different colours, a CSV file containing all track coordinates, a summary file with post processing data, such as average velocities and directionality, and preliminary plots of these quantities (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the computational performance of the software.

claim: KymoButler generates several output files including a dilated overlay image, a CSV file containing track coordinates, a summary file with post processing data, and preliminary plots.
source: After the computation, which takes 1–20 s per kymograph (depending on complexity), KymoButler generates several files including a dilated overlay image highlighting all the tracks found in different colours, a CSV file containing all track coordinates, a summary file with post processing data, such as average velocities and directionality, and preliminary plots of these quantities (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the output files generated by the software.

claim: KymoButler worked well on previously published kymographs from a variety of different biological data.
source: KymoButler worked well on previously published kymographs from a variety of different biological data (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) and on unpublished data from collaborators (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on testing shown in multiple figures.

claim: The unidirectional module of KymoButler was compared to the KymographDirect package.
source: The unidirectional module of KymoButler was compared to an existing kymograph analysis software, which is based on Fourier filters, and which provided the best performance among publicly available software in our hands (KymographDirect package; Mangeol et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes the comparison methodology.

claim: KymoButler was able to correctly pick up ~80% of all tracks at an SNR as low as 1.1.
source: Remarkably, KymoButler was able to correctly pick up ~80% of all tracks at an SNR as low as 1.1, where tracks are barely visible by eye (Figure 1—figure supplement 5B,D), and at high particle densities (~70% of the kymograph image covered with signal) (Figure 1—figure supplement 5F,H).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from testing at low SNR.

claim: KymoButler performed well at high particle densities (~70% of the kymograph image covered with signal).
source: Remarkably, KymoButler was able to correctly pick up ~80% of all tracks at an SNR as low as 1.1, where tracks are barely visible by eye (Figure 1—figure supplement 5B,D), and at high particle densities (~70% of the kymograph image covered with signal) (Figure 1—figure supplement 5F,H).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from testing at high particle density.

claim: Manual annotation at low SNR and high particle densities performed similarly to KymoButler.
source: Manual annotation at such extremes performed similarly to KymoButler (Figure 1—figure supplement 5C,D,G,H).
evidence: This is a comparative result from benchmarking experiments.

claim: KymoButler was able to reliably track particle traces in kymographs at low SNR and high particle densities in both synthetic and real data.
source: In summary, KymoButler was able to reliably track particle traces in kymographs at low SNR and high particle densities in both synthetic and real data, and it clearly outperformed currently existing automated software, while being as consistent as manual expert analysis while being ~100 x faster.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the benchmarking results.

claim: KymoButler clearly outperformed currently existing automated software.
source: In summary, KymoButler was able to reliably track particle traces in kymographs at low SNR and high particle densities in both synthetic and real data, and it clearly outperformed currently existing automated software, while being as consistent as manual expert analysis while being ~100 x faster.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the benchmarking results.

claim: KymoButler is as consistent as manual expert analysis while being ~100 x faster.
source: In summary, KymoButler was able to reliably track particle traces in kymographs at low SNR and high particle densities in both synthetic and real data, and it clearly outperformed currently existing automated software, while being as consistent as manual expert analysis while being ~100 x faster.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the benchmarking results.

claim: A custom-written wavelet coefficient filtering algorithm was implemented to compare the FCN-based approach to a more traditional non-ML approach for bidirectional kymographs.
source: Available fully automated software that relied on edge detection performed very poorly on our synthetic kymographs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1). Therefore, we implemented a custom-written wavelet coefficient filtering algorithm to compare our FCN-based approach to a more traditional non-ML approach (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the implementation of a comparison method.

claim: KymoButler performs well on both unidirectional and bidirectional kymographs.
source: Overall, these results showed that KymoButler performs well on both unidirectional and bidirectional kymographs, clearly outperforms currently available automated analysis of kymographs, and it performs as well as manual tracing, while being much faster and not prone to unconscious bias.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the benchmarking results.

claim: KymoButler clearly outperforms currently available automated analysis of kymographs.
source: Overall, these results showed that KymoButler performs well on both unidirectional and bidirectional kymographs, clearly outperforms currently available automated analysis of kymographs, and it performs as well as manual tracing, while being much faster and not prone to unconscious bias.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the benchmarking results.

claim: KymoButler performs as well as manual tracing, while being much faster and not prone to unconscious bias.
source: Overall, these results showed that KymoButler performs well on both unidirectional and bidirectional kymographs, clearly outperforms currently available automated analysis of kymographs, and it performs as well as manual tracing, while being much faster and not prone to unconscious bias.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the benchmarking results.

claim: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are nowadays widely applied for image recognition.
source: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are nowadays widely applied for image recognition.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of the field.

claim: The KymoButler software has only one adjustable detection parameter that is left to the user: a sensitivity threshold.
source: The KymoButler software has only one adjustable detection parameter that is left to the user: a sensitivity threshold that, if low, allows more ambiguous tracks to be recognised, and if high discards them.
evidence: This describes the user-adjustable parameters of the software.

claim: For synthetic data, the best value for the threshold lay between 0.1 and 0.3.
source: For our synthetic data, the best value for the threshold lay between 0.1 and 0.3 (Figure 1—figure supplement 4), and we observed a similar range for a variety of kymographs from published data.
evidence: This is based on empirical testing shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: The threshold depends on the SNR of the input images.
source: However, the threshold depends on the SNR of the input images, so that the correct threshold has to be chosen based on each biological application and imaging conditions.
evidence: This is an observation about the parameter dependency.

claim: The performance of both KymoButler and manual annotation decreased with decreasing SNR and increasing particle density.
source: Furthermore, the performance of both KymoButler and manual annotation decreased with decreasing SNR and increasing particle density (number of crossings in the image, Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is based on empirical testing shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Most of the publicly available kymograph analysis software requires manual labelling to extract quantitative data.
source: Most of the publicly available kymograph analysis software requires manual labelling to extract quantitative data (Chenouard, 2010; Neumann et al., 2017; Zala et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to existing software.

claim: Some automated approaches have been published in the context of specific biological questions, but these programs are currently not publicly available.
source: Some automated approaches have been published in the context of specific biological questions, but since these programs are currently not publicly available it is not clear how well they would perform on kymographs from other applications (Mukherjee et al., 2011; Reis et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: KymoButler is fully automated and able to reliably analyze kymographs from a wide range of biological applications.
source: As KymoButler is fully automated and able to reliably analyze kymographs from a wide range of biological applications, it fills an important gap.
evidence: This is a summary claim about the capabilities of the software.

claim: KymoButler is able to quantify mitochondria movement in neuronal dendrites, microtubule growth dynamics in axons, and in vitro dynamics of single cytoplasmic dynein proteins.
source: Here we showed that KymoButler is able to quantify mitochondria movement in neuronal dendrites, microtubule growth dynamics in axons, and in vitro dynamics of single cytoplasmic dynein proteins (Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on testing shown in figures.

claim: The training and validation data for KymoButler comprised kymographs depicting the dynamics of microtubule +ends, mitochondria movement, molecular motor movements, and vesicle transport in neuronal processes.
source: The training and validation data for KymoButler comprised kymographs depicting the dynamics of microtubule +ends, mitochondria movement, molecular motor movements, and vesicle transport in neuronal processes (example kymographs: Lazarus et al., 2013; Cioni et al., 2019; Hangen et al., 2018; Gerson-Gurwitz et al., 2011).
evidence: This describes the composition of the training dataset with citations.

claim: KymoButler will perform best on data similar to its training data.
source: Hence, KymoButler will perform best on similar data.
evidence: This is an inference based on the training data composition.

claim: KymoButler can be applied to most other kymographs obtained from time-lapse fluorescence microscopy without the need of any modifications.
source: However, we predict that it can furthermore be applied to most other kymographs obtained from time-lapse fluorescence microscopy without the need of any modifications.
evidence: This is a prediction about the generalizability of the software.

claim: KymoButler outperformed Fourier filtering, edge detection, and customised wavelet coefficient selection on synthetic kymographs.
source: KymoButler outperformed Fourier filtering, edge detection, and customised wavelet coefficient selection on synthetic kymographs.
evidence: This is a summary of the benchmarking results.

claim: Fourier filtering performed ~30% worse than KymoButler on synthetic unidirectional kymographs.
source: While Fourier filtering 'only' performed ~30% worse than KymoButler on synthetic unidirectional kymographs, edge detection on synthetic bidirectional kymographs suffered greatly from background fluctuations and low SNR to such an extent that the extracted data was unusable (see Figure 3—figure supplement 1 for one example).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison based on benchmarking results.

claim: Edge detection on synthetic bidirectional kymographs suffered greatly from background fluctuations and low SNR to such an extent that the extracted data was unusable.
source: While Fourier filtering 'only' performed ~30% worse than KymoButler on synthetic unidirectional kymographs, edge detection on synthetic bidirectional kymographs suffered greatly from background fluctuations and low SNR to such an extent that the extracted data was unusable (see Figure 3—figure supplement 1 for one example).
evidence: This is based on testing shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: KymoButler performed 20% better than the wavelet filtering approach on synthetic bidirectional kymographs.
source: KymoButler still performed 20% better than this approach (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison based on benchmarking results.

claim: The main problem with filtering approaches compared to KymoButler was their inability to bridge track gaps and resolve line crossings.
source: The main problem with either filtering approach compared to KymoButler was their inability to bridge track gaps and resolve line crossings, both of which occur frequently in biological data (Figures 2C,D and 3C,D).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the benchmarking results shown in figures.

claim: KymoButler performed as well as expert annotation, but within a much shorter time.
source: These challenges were met by KymoButler, which performed as well as expert annotation, but within a much shorter time (Figures 2 and 3).
evidence: This is a summary of the benchmarking results shown in figures.

claim: Synthetic kymographs will reproduce the complexity of real kymographs only to some degree.
source: Synthetic kymographs, however, will reproduce the complexity of real kymographs only to some degree, as they exhibit homogenous background, no artefacts, no varying particle intensity in time, and individual tracks can appear rather similar.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of synthetic data.

claim: Values obtained from manual annotation deviated by up to 20% from ground truth values on synthetic data.
source: However, since values obtained from manual annotation deviated by up to 20% from ground truth values on synthetic data, deviations from manual annotation should not automatically be interpreted as an erroneous deviation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the benchmarking results shown in figures.

claim: KymoButler is able to correctly identify individual full-length tracks in kymographs with an average track F1 score of 92% on unidirectional tracks and 78% on complex bidirectional tracks.
source: Our results show that KymoButler is able to correctly identify individual full-length tracks in kymographs with an average track F1 score (geometric mean of track precision and recall) of 92% on unidirectional tracks and 78% on complex bidirectional tracks (similar to manual annotation), without suffering from inconsistency, bias, and laborious tracing, that plague manual tracking.
evidence: This is a summary of the quantitative performance results.

claim: KymoButler does not suffer from inconsistency, bias, and laborious tracing that plague manual tracking.
source: Our results show that KymoButler is able to correctly identify individual full-length tracks in kymographs with an average track F1 score (geometric mean of track precision and recall) of 92% on unidirectional tracks and 78% on complex bidirectional tracks (similar to manual annotation), without suffering from inconsistency, bias, and laborious tracing, that plague manual tracking.
evidence: This is a claimed advantage of automated analysis.

claim: Users have the option to anonymously upload kymographs to the cloud when using the webform.
source: Every time someone uses our webform, s/he has the option to anonymously upload the kymograph to our cloud.
evidence: This describes a feature of the web application.

claim: Uploaded kymographs will be annotated and added to the training data to improve KymoButler.
source: Once a large number of diverse kymographs is uploaded, these kymographs will be annotated by us and added to our training data, improving KymoButler even further.
evidence: This describes a planned future improvement strategy.

claim: A similar approach to KymoButler could stack the frames of a 2D/3D movie on top of each other to generate a 3D/4D kymogram.
source: A similar, albeit computationally heavier, approach could stack the frames of a 2D/3D movie on top of each other to generate a 3D/4D kymogram (2D space and time, or 3D space and time).
evidence: This is a speculation about future extensions of the approach.

claim: Previously generated kymograms have led to intriguing results on whole-cell particle tracking problems with high SNR.
source: Previously generated kymograms have led to intriguing results on whole-cell particle tracking problems with high SNR (Racine et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation.

claim: The use of higher dimensional FCNs in the future has great potential to yield human-like performance on any biological and medical tracking problems.
source: The use of higher dimensional FCNs in the future has great potential to yield human-like performance on any biological and medical tracking problems.
evidence: This is a speculation about future applications.

claim: All code was written in the wolfram language in Mathematica.
source: All code was written in the wolfram language in Mathematica https://wolfram.com/mathematica and, if not stated otherwise, can be found online under: https://github.com/MaxJakobs/KymoButler (copy archived at swh:1:rev:e35173e9051eb5395f9b13dcd8f487ffa4098592).
evidence: This describes the implementation details.

claim: The KymoButler software was implemented in Mathematica to take advantage of easy web form deployment and distribution.
source: The KymoButler software was implemented in Mathematica to take advantage of easy web form deployment and distribution.
evidence: This describes the rationale for the implementation choice.

claim: Batch normalisation is useful to stabilise the training procedure as it rescales the inputs of the activation function.
source: Batch normalisation is useful to stabilise the training procedure as it rescales the inputs of the activation function (leakyReLu), so that they have zero mean and unit variance.
evidence: This describes the function of batch normalisation.

claim: The leakyReLu prevents the so-called 'dead ReLu's' by applying a small gradient to values below 0.
source: The leakyReLu prevents the so-called 'dead ReLu's' by applying a small gradient to values below 0.
evidence: This describes the function of the leakyReLu activation.

claim: These building blocks were previously used for image recognition tasks in Google's inception architecture and in the U-Net architecture.
source: These building blocks were previously used for image recognition tasks in Google's inception architecture and in the U-Net architecture (Szegedy, 2014; Falk et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: The classification module takes a resized kymograph of size 64 × 64 pixels and generates two output values that correspond to the class probabilities for unidirectional/bidirectional kymographs.
source: The classification module takes a resized kymograph of size 64 × 64 pixels and generates two output values that correspond to the class probabilities for unidirectional/bidirectional kymographs (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This describes the architecture of the classification module.

claim: Due to the U-Net architecture, each dimension of the inputs to the segmentation modules needs to be a multiple of 16.
source: Due to the U-Net architecture, each dimension of the inputs to the segmentation modules needs to be a multiple of 16.
evidence: This describes a constraint of the network architecture.

claim: All network training was performed on a workstation, using a nVidia 1080 Ti or a nVidia 1070 GPU.
source: All network training was performed on a workstation, using a nVidia 1080 Ti or a nVidia 1070 GPU.
evidence: This describes the computational resources used.

claim: The class module was trained until the validation set error rate was consistently 0%.
source: The final input image was randomly cropped to 64 × 64 pixels (see examples Figure 1—figure supplement 3A) and the class module was trained using stochastic gradient descent (ADAM optimiser, Kingma, 2017, initial learning rate 0.001), until the validation set error rate was consistently 0%.
evidence: This describes the training stopping criterion.

claim: Synthetic data was generated by simulating individual particles on a stationary path of length 300 pixels for 300 frames to generate 300 × 300 pixel kymographs.
source: Synthetic data was generated by simulating individual particles on a stationary path of length 300 pixels for 300 frames to generate 300 × 300 pixel kymographs.
evidence: This describes the synthetic data generation methodology.

claim: The resulting synthetic kymographs and movies had an average signal-to-noise ratio of 1.2 for unidirectional data.
source: The resulting kymographs and movies had an average signal-to-noise ratio of 1.2 (calculated as the average intensity of the signal, divided by the average intensity of the background).
evidence: This describes a characteristic of the synthetic data.

claim: The resulting synthetic kymographs and movies had an average signal-to-noise ratio of 1.4 for bidirectional data.
source: The resulting kymographs and movies had an average signal-to-noise ratio of 1.4.
evidence: This describes a characteristic of the synthetic data.

claim: Track recall is calculated as the fractional overlap between each ground truth track and its corresponding predicted track.
source: To calculate track recall, each ground truth track was first compared to its corresponding predicted track, and the fractional overlap between them was calculated.
evidence: This describes the methodology for calculating track recall.

claim: Track precision is calculated by finding the largest ground truth track that corresponds to each prediction and calculating the fraction of the predicted track that overlaps with the ground truth track.
source: Track precision was calculated by finding the largest ground truth track that corresponded, that is had the largest overlap, to each prediction, and then calculating the fraction of the predicted track that overlapped to the ground truth track.
evidence: This describes the methodology for calculating track precision.

claim: The track F1 score is calculated as the geometric mean of the average track recall and the average track precision.
source: We then calculated the geometric mean of the average track recall and the average track precision (the 'track F1 score', see Materials and methods) for each kymograph (Figure 2E).
evidence: This describes the methodology for calculating the F1 score.
